method: Social jetlag is the difference between the midpoint of sleep on workdays and on free days, following Wittmann and colleagues (2006): the midpoint of an episode is its bedtime plus half its length, taken modulo 24 hours. Bed and wake times are read as strict 24-hour HH:MM values, so an hour above 23, a minute above 59 or a non-zero seconds part is refused, while a trailing :00 is accepted; the sleep length is the clockwise distance from bedtime to wake time, adding 24 hours when the window crosses midnight. Identical bed and wake times, and windows longer than 16 hours, are refused with the computed length named in the message. Because half of an odd number of minutes falls on a half minute, the displayed mid-sleep times and the shift are rounded to the nearest minute while the arithmetic keeps the exact value. The shift is free-day mid-sleep minus workday mid-sleep, wrapped into the interval from -12 to +12 hours so that the shorter way round the clock is reported; exactly 12 hours is reported as later because the direction is then ambiguous, and a warning says so. The tool also reports both sleep lengths, their signed difference and a warning when free-day sleep is at least an hour longer, because the uncorrected midpoint then mixes a later body clock with recovery sleep. Daylight saving, travel, naps and device measurements never enter the calculation, and nothing is uploaded, stored or sent. This is time arithmetic on self-reported clock times, not a medical measurement or advice.

sources.title: Wittmann, Dinich, Merrow & Roenneberg — Social jetlag: misalignment of biological and social time, Chronobiology International 23(1-2):497-509 (2006)
